## From text to a reusable model {#overview .overview-slide .two-session-overview}

![](images/pretraining-overview.png){.overview-image fig-alt="Original conceptual overview: documents become tokens, which branch into missing-token and next-token prediction tasks. Both feed a model with a learning loop. The learned model connects to downstream applications represented by classification groups, document search, and conversation."}

<div class="session-overview-route">
<div><span class="session-tag">SESSION 1 · LEARN</span><strong>Text → prediction → learned weights</strong><p>Build training targets. Compare BERT, GPT, and T5.</p></div>
<div><span class="session-tag">SESSION 2 · REUSE</span><strong>Learned weights → useful tasks</strong><p>Fine-tune with labels, or prompt with fixed weights.</p></div>
</div>
<p class="overview-caption">Conceptual illustration · applications can require further adaptation; pretraining alone does not produce an assistant.</p>

::: {.notes}
Trace the image from left to right. The documents supply observed text. The upper
branch suggests a missing token; the lower branch suggests the next token. The
loop changes model parameters. Session 1 opens this learning process and also
introduces T5's missing-span recipe, which is not separately drawn in the image.

Then point to the applications. They are examples of possible uses, not immediate
capabilities guaranteed by pretraining. Session 2 follows the learned weights into
classification, token labeling, question answering, and prompted generation.
Document search is shown as an application in the overview, but its full pipeline
belongs to the later RAG lecture. This artwork is schematic, not measured evidence.
:::

## Session 1 · How does pretraining work? {#session-1 .session-contents}

<p class="session-lead">How can raw text supply both the questions and the answers?</p>
<div class="session-agenda">
<div><b>01</b><strong>Why pretrain?</strong><span>From word embeddings to a contextual model.</span><em>15 min</em></div>
<div><b>02</b><strong>Text supplies its own targets</strong><span>Construct prediction examples without manual labels.</span><em>15 min</em></div>
<div><b>03</b><strong>BERT: recover hidden tokens</strong><span>Masking, 80/10/10 corruption, and one worked loss.</span><em>30 min</em></div>
<div><b>04</b><strong>GPT: pretrain a causal LM</strong><span>Familiar AR objective → reusable weights; compare supervision.</span><em>12 min</em></div>
<div><b>05</b><strong>T5: reconstruct missing spans</strong><span>Read a corrupted source; generate its gaps.</span><em>15 min</em></div>
<div><b>06</b><strong>One sentence, three recipes</strong><span>Build and compare the inputs and targets together.</span><em>15 min</em></div>
</div>
<p class="session-budget">102 minutes of teaching and activities + 18 minutes for questions or a break.</p>
<p class="route-question">We trained a word predictor. How can it become a sentiment classifier?</p>

::: {.notes}
These times are a pacing proposal, including short student questions and one
numerical exercise; do not add activities on top of the revised 102-minute plan.

Use Stanford's PDF pages 10–11 for embedding-only versus whole-model pretraining,
and page 19 for the complete pretrain/fine-tune workflow. Use Berkeley PDF pages
36 and 58 as a matched visual pair for masked and causal prediction. Stanford
PDF page 36 and Berkeley page 66 supply the T5 span-corruption illustrations.
Page references are PDF viewer pages, not Stanford's printed slide numbers.

Keep one small example visible when introducing each rule. The original BERT
recipe selects 15% of eligible positions; the 80/10/10 probabilities apply within
that selected set. Reuse previous-draft.qmd#bert-corruption and the separate
PAUSE/solution pair at #bert-loss-pause and #bert-loss-solution. No arithmetic
answer should appear on its prompt slide. Mention NSP briefly as historical context.

End the completed session with a visual bridge from pretrained weights to a new
sentiment task. This contents slide previews that question; it is not the final
session-ending visual. The approved first two sections and architecture orientation are followed by
the BERT section and a focused GPT pretraining increment. T5 and the synthesis now complete Session 1; stop at the sentiment-adaptation bridge.
:::
